claim: Trrap-PCΔ mice were born healthy and exhibited normal motor coordination at young age (1–2 months) in rotarod tests.
source: Trrap-PCΔ mice were born healthy and exhibited normal (in rotarod tests) or mild defective (in beam balance) motor coordination at young age (1–2 months).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the motor coordination performance of young Trrap-PCΔ mice in rotarod tests.

claim: Trrap-PCΔ mice exhibited mild defective motor coordination at young age (1–2 months) in beam balance tests.
source: Trrap-PCΔ mice were born healthy and exhibited normal (in rotarod tests) or mild defective (in beam balance) motor coordination at young age (1–2 months).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the motor coordination performance of young Trrap-PCΔ mice in beam balance tests.

claim: Trrap-PCΔ mice displayed evident miscoordination at mid age (3–6 months).
source: However, they displayed an evident miscoordination at mid age (3–6 months), which became more severe after 9 months (old group) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1A showing motor coordination test results.

claim: Trrap-PCΔ mice developed age-dependent locomotor dysfunction characterized by signs of ataxia by the age of 1 year.
source: By the age of 1 year, Trrap-PCΔ mice developed an age-dependent locomotor dysfunction characterized by signs of ataxia, namely impaired coordination and unsteady gait (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the phenotype observed in 1-year-old Trrap-PCΔ mice.

claim: Trrap-PCΔ mice show progressive loss of Purkinje cells starting from 3 months old.
source: Immunostaining of the Purkinje cell marker calbindin revealed a progressive loss of Purkinje cells in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella – starting from 3 months old mice – which became severe at 9 months (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1B,C showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Purkinje cell loss in Trrap-PCΔ mice became severe at 9 months.
source: Immunostaining of the Purkinje cell marker calbindin revealed a progressive loss of Purkinje cells in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella – starting from 3 months old mice – which became severe at 9 months (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1B,C showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed progressive Purkinje cell loss in Trrap-PCΔ brains as judged by downregulation of calbindin.
source: Western blot analysis of mutant brains of different ages confirmed a progressive Purkinje cell loss, as judged by the downregulation of calbindin (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1D,E showing western blot data.

claim: There was no significant change in the expression of the oligodendrocyte marker CNPase in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella.
source: While there was no significant change in the expression of the oligodendrocyte marker CNPase, a progressive increase of the astrocyte marker GFAP, namely astrogliosis, and the activated microglia marker Galectin-3 were evident in mutant cerebella, both of which are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding and references Figure 1D,E showing western blot data.

claim: A progressive increase of the astrocyte marker GFAP (astrogliosis) was evident in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella.
source: While there was no significant change in the expression of the oligodendrocyte marker CNPase, a progressive increase of the astrocyte marker GFAP, namely astrogliosis, and the activated microglia marker Galectin-3 were evident in mutant cerebella, both of which are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding and references Figure 1D,E showing western blot data.

claim: A progressive increase of the activated microglia marker Galectin-3 was evident in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella.
source: While there was no significant change in the expression of the oligodendrocyte marker CNPase, a progressive increase of the astrocyte marker GFAP, namely astrogliosis, and the activated microglia marker Galectin-3 were evident in mutant cerebella, both of which are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding and references Figure 1D,E showing western blot data.

claim: Astrogliosis and activated microglia are hallmarks of neurodegeneration.
source: While there was no significant change in the expression of the oligodendrocyte marker CNPase, a progressive increase of the astrocyte marker GFAP, namely astrogliosis, and the activated microglia marker Galectin-3 were evident in mutant cerebella, both of which are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge in the context of interpreting the findings.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed a loss of Purkinje cells in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella at old age (9 months).
source: Immunostaining of the cerebella of 2-month-old and 9-month-old mice confirmed a loss of Purkinje cells and a great increase of astrocytes (GFAP+ signals), a sign of astrogliosis, in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella at old age, whereas Trrap-PCΔ cerebella of young mice were normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed a great increase of astrocytes (GFAP+ signals) in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella at old age (9 months).
source: Immunostaining of the cerebella of 2-month-old and 9-month-old mice confirmed a loss of Purkinje cells and a great increase of astrocytes (GFAP+ signals), a sign of astrogliosis, in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella at old age, whereas Trrap-PCΔ cerebella of young mice were normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Trrap-PCΔ cerebella of young mice (2 months) were normal.
source: Immunostaining of the cerebella of 2-month-old and 9-month-old mice confirmed a loss of Purkinje cells and a great increase of astrocytes (GFAP+ signals), a sign of astrogliosis, in Trrap-PCΔ cerebella at old age, whereas Trrap-PCΔ cerebella of young mice were normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: TUNEL staining detected more cell death in all cerebellar lobes of old Trrap-PCΔ mice.
source: Also, TUNEL staining detected more cell death in all cerebellar lobes of old mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Axonal swellings of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells were detected at 1 month of age, prior to Purkinje cell loss.
source: Immunostaining of brain sections using antibodies against calbindin and myelin-binding protein (MBP) detected axonal swellings of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells readily at 1 month of age, prior to Purkinje cell loss (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A showing immunostaining.

claim: Axonal swellings in Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells were generally myelinated at 1 month of age.
source: Axonal swellings were generally myelinated at this age (Figure 2A), although a loss of myelination was observed occasionally in a few severe cases (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A.

claim: A loss of myelination was observed occasionally in a few severe cases of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells at 1 month of age.
source: Axonal swellings were generally myelinated at this age (Figure 2A), although a loss of myelination was observed occasionally in a few severe cases (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation.

claim: The myelination index of Purkinje cell axons was normal in young (1-month-old) Trrap-PCΔ mice.
source: Furthermore, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed the myelination index of Purkinje cell axons as normal in young (1-month-old) mice, but significantly lower, as judged by a higher g-ratio, in mid age (6-month-old) Trrap-PCΔ mice compared to controls (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2B,C showing TEM data.

claim: The myelination index of Purkinje cell axons was significantly lower in mid age (6-month-old) Trrap-PCΔ mice compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed the myelination index of Purkinje cell axons as normal in young (1-month-old) mice, but significantly lower, as judged by a higher g-ratio, in mid age (6-month-old) Trrap-PCΔ mice compared to controls (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2B,C showing TEM data.

claim: A higher g-ratio indicates a lower myelination index.
source: Furthermore, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed the myelination index of Purkinje cell axons as normal in young (1-month-old) mice, but significantly lower, as judged by a higher g-ratio, in mid age (6-month-old) Trrap-PCΔ mice compared to controls (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The manuscript explains the interpretation of g-ratio measurements.

claim: Sholl analysis showed a progressive decrease in the size of dendritic trees of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells from young age (1–4 months) to old age (10 months).
source: A Sholl analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells at young age (1–4 months) and at old age (10 months) showed a progressive decrease in the size of their dendritic trees without great effects on their complexity as judged by the critical value (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references multiple figures showing Sholl analysis results.

claim: Trrap deletion did not have great effects on the complexity of Purkinje cell dendritic trees as judged by the critical value.
source: A Sholl analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells at young age (1–4 months) and at old age (10 months) showed a progressive decrease in the size of their dendritic trees without great effects on their complexity as judged by the critical value (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references multiple figures showing Sholl analysis results.

claim: The molecular layer became thinner at older age compared to young age in Trrap-PCΔ mice.
source: Consistent with the Sholl analysis data, the molecular layer became thinner at older age compared to young age (Figure 2G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Trrap deletion does not affect arborization, but rather causes a retraction of already formed dendrites of neurons.
source: These observations indicate that Trrap deletion does not affect arborization, but rather causes a retraction of already formed dendrites of neurons.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the Sholl analysis and molecular layer thickness data.

claim: Trrap-FBΔ brains were normal and had an efficient deletion of Trrap at day 10 of postnatal life (P10).
source: Trrap-FBΔ brains were normal and had an efficient deletion of Trrap already at day 10 of the postnatal life (P10) (Figure 3A, see below for protein analysis in Figure 4A,B, and for qPCR analysis Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references multiple figures showing the deletion efficiency.

claim: Trrap deletion resulted in 5090 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in cortices (cutoff adjusted, p<0.05).
source: Trrap deletion resulted in highly reproducible changes in the transcriptome of cortices and striata with 5090 and 4389 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) respectively (cutoff adjusted, p<0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from RNA-seq analysis and references figures and supplementary files.

claim: Trrap deletion resulted in 4389 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in striata (cutoff adjusted, p<0.05).
source: Trrap deletion resulted in highly reproducible changes in the transcriptome of cortices and striata with 5090 and 4389 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) respectively (cutoff adjusted, p<0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from RNA-seq analysis and references figures and supplementary files.

claim: The Trrap-FBΔ cortex and striatum shared 2695 common DEGs, corresponding to 52.9% and 61.4% of the respective tissues.
source: The Trrap-FBΔ cortex and striatum shared 2695 common DEGs, corresponding to 52.9% and 61.4% of the respective tissues.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from the comparison of RNA-seq data.

claim: The directionality of the changes was conserved in 99.3% of the common DEGs between cortex and striatum.
source: The directionality of the changes was conserved in 99.3% of the genes (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3C and supplementary file.

claim: Among the common DEGs, 1122 upregulated and 1554 downregulated genes were overlapping between cortex and striatum.
source: Among the common DEGs, 1122 upregulated and 1554 downregulated genes were overlapping between these two parts of the brain (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3C.

claim: Similar mechanisms operate in the neurons from both cortex and striatum brain regions.
source: These results strongly suggest that similar mechanisms operate in the neurons from both brain regions.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the high overlap and directionality conservation of DEGs.

claim: About half of the Top50 pathways from GO analyses of common DEGs were linked with microtubule dynamics and its related cellular processes.
source: Intriguingly, about a half of the Top50 pathways were linked with microtubule dynamics and its related cellular processes (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from GO analysis and references Figure 3D.

claim: Sp1 activity was dramatically decreased in Trrap-deleted NSCs compared to control cells.
source: Using these cells, we then performed a luciferase reporter assay to investigate whether Sp1 is directly regulated by Trrap and detected a dramatic decrease in Sp1 activity in Trrap-deleted NSCs, compared to control cells.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from luciferase reporter assay.

claim: Ectopic overexpression of Sp1 in Trrap-deleted cells failed to activate the Sp1-reporter.
source: Strikingly, ectopic overexpression of Sp1 in Trrap-deleted cells failed to activate the Sp1-reporter (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3F showing luciferase assay results.

claim: Trrap is required for Sp1-mediated transcriptional activation.
source: These data indicate that Trrap is indeed required for Sp1-mediated transcriptional activation.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the luciferase assay results.

claim: More than 30% of the Top50 pathways under the control of Sp1 were linked with microtubule dynamics-related cellular processes.
source: GO analysis of the common DEGs revealed that more than 30% of the Top50 pathways under the control of Sp1 were linked with microtubule dynamics-related cellular processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2g, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from GO analysis and references figure and supplementary file.

claim: Depletion of Trrap led to a downregulation of 2274 AcH3 peaks associated with coding genes.
source: Depletion of Trrap led to a downregulation of 2274 AcH3 and 1355 AcH4 peaks that were associated with coding genes (equivalent to 10% of the most depleted regions in TrrapΔ versus controls) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP-seq analysis and references figure and supplementary file.

claim: Depletion of Trrap led to a downregulation of 1355 AcH4 peaks associated with coding genes.
source: Depletion of Trrap led to a downregulation of 2274 AcH3 and 1355 AcH4 peaks that were associated with coding genes (equivalent to 10% of the most depleted regions in TrrapΔ versus controls) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP-seq analysis and references figure and supplementary file.

claim: Only 12.6% of depleted AcH3 peaks correlated with changes in the RNA level of the corresponding genes in Trrap-FBΔ brains.
source: Only 12.6% and 10.2% respectively of these depleted peaks correlated with changes in the RNA level of the corresponding genes in Trrap-FBΔ brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Only 10.2% of depleted AcH4 peaks correlated with changes in the RNA level of the corresponding genes in Trrap-FBΔ brains.
source: Only 12.6% and 10.2% respectively of these depleted peaks correlated with changes in the RNA level of the corresponding genes in Trrap-FBΔ brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: ChIP-seq analyses revealed no significant difference of AcH3 on Sp1-site between control and Trrap-deleted aNSCs.
source: ChIP-seq analyses revealed no significant difference of AcH3 on Sp1-site between control and Trrap-deleted aNSCs, whereas H4Ac on Sp1-site in control (mean = 12.37) is slightly lower than in Trrap mutants (mean = 12.54) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP-seq analysis and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: H4Ac on Sp1-site in control aNSCs (mean = 12.37) is slightly lower than in Trrap mutants (mean = 12.54).
source: ChIP-seq analyses revealed no significant difference of AcH3 on Sp1-site between control and Trrap-deleted aNSCs, whereas H4Ac on Sp1-site in control (mean = 12.37) is slightly lower than in Trrap mutants (mean = 12.54) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP-seq analysis and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The downregulated genes had a significantly lower acetylation level of H3 and H4 in the Sp1 promoter area in Trrap deleted cells.
source: Interestingly, the downregulated genes had a significantly lower acetylation level of H3 and H4 in the Sp1 promoter area in Trrap deleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP-seq analysis and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Twenty-two genes exhibited downregulated histone H3 and H4 acetylation and were also downregulated in the RNA-seq from brains.
source: Twenty-two genes exhibited downregulated histone H3 and H4 acetylation and were also downregulated in the RNA-seq from brains.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Among the 22 genes with downregulated histone H3 and H4 acetylation and RNA levels, 11 genes were Sp1 targets according to the Harmonizome database.
source: Among them, 11 genes were Sp1 targets according to the Harmonizome database (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from comparison with the Harmonizome database.

claim: Microtubule dynamics have been proposed to be involved in brain homeostasis.
source: The microtubule dynamics proteins STMN3 (SCLIP) and STMN4 (RB3) are of special interest (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e), because microtubule dynamics have been proposed to be involved in brain homeostasis (Chauvin and Sobel, 2015; Dubey et al., 2015) and defects in microtubule dynamics often cause axonal swellings and dendrite retraction in postmitotic neurons (Dubey et al., 2015; Voelzmann et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Defects in microtubule dynamics often cause axonal swellings and dendrite retraction in postmitotic neurons.
source: The microtubule dynamics proteins STMN3 (SCLIP) and STMN4 (RB3) are of special interest (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e), because microtubule dynamics have been proposed to be involved in brain homeostasis (Chauvin and Sobel, 2015; Dubey et al., 2015) and defects in microtubule dynamics often cause axonal swellings and dendrite retraction in postmitotic neurons (Dubey et al., 2015; Voelzmann et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: STMNs 3 and 4 were found within the Top30 changes in RNA-seq and proteomics data sets of brain samples.
source: STMNs 3 and 4 were found within the Top30 changes in our RNA-seq and proteomics data sets of brain samples (Source data 1B and C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from RNA-seq and proteomics analysis.

claim: qPCR analysis confirmed a great downregulation of STMN3 and STMN4 in Trrap deleted cells of forebrain tissues.
source: qPCR analysis confirmed a great downregulation of these genes in Trrap deleted cells of forebrain tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed a great reduction of both STMN3 and STMN4 proteins in Trrap-deleted forebrains at P10.
source: Western blot analysis also confirmed a great reduction of both STMN3 and STMN4 proteins in Trrap-deleted forebrains at P10 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4A,B.

claim: Co-staining detected a significant decrease of both STMN3 and STMN4 in Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells compared to controls.
source: Co-staining of STMN3 or STMN4 with calbindin in the brain sections detected a significant decrease of both proteins in Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells compared to controls (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4C,D.

claim: ChIP-seq showed that the level of AcH3 and AcH4 at the promoters of STMN3 and STMN4 was greatly reduced in Trrap-deleted cells.
source: To explore the mechanism, ChIP-seq was performed and showed that the level of AcH3 and AcH4 at the promoters of these genes was greatly reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Both Sp1 binding and histone H4 acetylation were enriched at the STMN3 and STMN4 promoters in control brain samples.
source: To validate the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, we performed ChIP experiments in brain samples and found both Sp1 binding and histone H4 acetylation were enriched at the STMN3 and STMN4 promoters in controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4E.

claim: Upon Trrap deletion there was a dramatic decrease in Sp1 binding at the STMN3 and STMN4 promoters.
source: Upon Trrap deletion there was a dramatic decrease in Sp1 binding, as well as in the acetylation of histone H4 in the STMN3 and STMN4 promoters (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4F,G.

claim: Upon Trrap deletion there was a dramatic decrease in the acetylation of histone H4 in the STMN3 and STMN4 promoters.
source: Upon Trrap deletion there was a dramatic decrease in Sp1 binding, as well as in the acetylation of histone H4 in the STMN3 and STMN4 promoters (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4F,G.

claim: Trrap deletion did not change the H3K4m2 level in the STMN3 promoter.
source: We also noted that Trrap deletion did not change the H3K4m2 level in the STMN3 promoter, yet decreased mildly in the STMN4 promoter.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP analysis.

claim: Trrap deletion decreased H3K4m2 level mildly in the STMN4 promoter.
source: We also noted that Trrap deletion did not change the H3K4m2 level in the STMN3 promoter, yet decreased mildly in the STMN4 promoter.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from ChIP analysis.

claim: Trrap deficiency did not compromise binding of Sp1-unrelated transcription factor Oct4 at the promoter proximities of STMN3 and STMN4 genes.
source: Moreover, Trrap deficiency did not compromise binding of Sp1-unrelated transcription factor Oct4 at the promoter proximities of these STMNs genes (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4F,G.

claim: Trrap is essential for loading Sp1 and HATs to the promoters of Sp1 target genes.
source: These data together indicate an essentiality of Trrap for loading Sp1 and HATs to the promoters of these Sp1 target genes.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the ChIP data.

claim: siRNA-mediated Sp1 knockdown decreased expression of STMN3 and STMN4 proteins.
source: Furthermore, siRNA-mediated Sp1 knockdown indeed decreased expression of STMN3 and STMN4 proteins (Figure 4H).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4H.

claim: The Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis directly controls the expression of STMN3 and STMN4 in neurons.
source: These results demonstrate that the Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis directly controls the expression of STMN3 and STMN4 in neurons.
evidence: The manuscript provides this conclusion based on the ChIP and knockdown experiments.

claim: Trrap knockdown evidently reduced the neurite length of primary neurons.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the Trrap knockdown evidently reduced the neurite length and the branching numbers of neurons (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5A–C.

claim: Trrap knockdown evidently reduced the branching numbers of primary neurons.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the Trrap knockdown evidently reduced the neurite length and the branching numbers of neurons (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5A–C.

claim: Trrap deficiency compromises neuronal arborization in vitro.
source: These findings indicate that Trrap deficiency also compromises neuronal arborization in vitro.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the neurite length and branching data.

claim: Ectopic expression of STMN3 is sufficient to rescue neuronal defects caused by Trrap knockdown.
source: Intriguingly, ectopic expression of STMN3 is sufficient to rescue these neuronal defects caused by Trrap knockdown (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5A,B.

claim: Ectopic expression of STMN4 corrected the neurite length and branching defects in Trrap knockdown primary neurons.
source: Similarly, ectopic expression of STMN4 also corrected the neurite length and branching defects in Trrap knockdown primary neurons (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5A,C.

claim: A co-upregulation of both STMNs occurs when either STMN3 or STMN4 was overexpressed.
source: Interestingly, we note a co-upregulation of both STMNs when either STMN3 or STMN4 was overexpressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e), which suggests a co-stabilization or cooperative action of both STMNs in microtubule dynamics in the brain; yet the underlying mechanism requires further investigation.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Trrap prevents neuropathy by regulating Stathmin associated with microtubule dynamics.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that Trrap prevents neuropathy by regulating Stathmin associated with microtubule dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript provides this conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Human patients carrying de novo mutations of TRRAP are associated with neuropathological symptoms, such as ID, ASD, and epilepsy.
source: Very recently, human patients carrying de novo mutations of TRRAP are reported to be associated with neuropathological symptoms, such as ID, ASD, and epilepsy (Cogné et al., 2019; Mavros et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published clinical studies.

claim: The Sp1 transcription regulation network by HAT is a plausible mechanism for TRRAP-associated neuropathies in humans.
source: Although molecular pathways have not been investigated in these genetic studies, our findings hint at the Sp1 transcription regulation network by HAT being a plausible mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript provides this speculation based on their findings and the human genetic studies.

claim: The Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis orchestrates the program of neuronal microtubule dynamics and neuron morphogenesis.
source: Our findings propose that the Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis orchestrates the program of neuronal microtubule dynamics and neuron morphogenesis and, possibly, neuron survival.
evidence: The manuscript provides this conclusion based on their integrated findings.

claim: The Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis possibly orchestrates neuron survival.
source: Our findings propose that the Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis orchestrates the program of neuronal microtubule dynamics and neuron morphogenesis and, possibly, neuron survival.
evidence: The manuscript provides this speculation based on their findings.

claim: Mutations of HAT cofactor TRRAP cause human neuropathies, including psychosis, intellectual disability, autism, and epilepsy.
source: Mutations of HAT cofactor TRRAP (transformation/transcription domain-associated protein) cause human neuropathies, including psychosis, intellectual disability, autism, and epilepsy, with unknown mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript states this in the abstract, citing known clinical associations.

claim: Trrap deletion in Purkinje neurons results in neurodegeneration of old mice.
source: Here we show that Trrap deletion in Purkinje neurons results in neurodegeneration of old mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: TRRAP via SP1 conducts a conserved transcriptomic program.
source: Integrated transcriptomics, epigenomics, and proteomics reveal that TRRAP via SP1 conducts a conserved transcriptomic program.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: TRRAP is required for SP1 binding at the promoter proximity of target genes, especially microtubule dynamics genes.
source: TRRAP is required for SP1 binding at the promoter proximity of target genes, especially microtubule dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: The ectopic expression of Stathmin3/4 ameliorates defects of TRRAP-deficient neurons.
source: The ectopic expression of Stathmin3/4 ameliorates defects of TRRAP-deficient neurons, indicating that the microtubule dynamics is particularly vulnerable to the action of SP1 activity.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: Microtubule dynamics is particularly vulnerable to the action of SP1 activity.
source: The ectopic expression of Stathmin3/4 ameliorates defects of TRRAP-deficient neurons, indicating that the microtubule dynamics is particularly vulnerable to the action of SP1 activity.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the rescue experiments.

claim: This study unravels a network linking TRRAP, HAT, and SP1 with microtubule dynamics in neuroprotection.
source: This study unravels a network linking three well-known, but up-to-date unconnected, signaling pathways, namely TRRAP, HAT, and SP1 with microtubule dynamics, in neuroprotection.
evidence: The manuscript states this as the main conclusion in the abstract.

claim: Progressive neuronal loss is a hallmark of neurodegeneration.
source: Progressive neuronal loss, synaptic deficits, disintegration of neuronal networks due to axonal and dendritic retraction, and failure of neurological functions are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Synaptic deficits are a hallmark of neurodegeneration.
source: Progressive neuronal loss, synaptic deficits, disintegration of neuronal networks due to axonal and dendritic retraction, and failure of neurological functions are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Disintegration of neuronal networks due to axonal and dendritic retraction is a hallmark of neurodegeneration.
source: Progressive neuronal loss, synaptic deficits, disintegration of neuronal networks due to axonal and dendritic retraction, and failure of neurological functions are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Failure of neurological functions is a hallmark of neurodegeneration.
source: Progressive neuronal loss, synaptic deficits, disintegration of neuronal networks due to axonal and dendritic retraction, and failure of neurological functions are hallmarks of neurodegeneration (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Molecular causes of neurodegeneration include protein misfolding and degradation.
source: Molecular causes of neurodegeneration are believed to include protein misfolding and degradation, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, DNA damage accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, as well as programmed cell death (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018; Kurtishi et al., 2019; Burté et al., 2015; Chi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Molecular causes of neurodegeneration include neuroinflammation.
source: Molecular causes of neurodegeneration are believed to include protein misfolding and degradation, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, DNA damage accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, as well as programmed cell death (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018; Kurtishi et al., 2019; Burté et al., 2015; Chi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Molecular causes of neurodegeneration include oxidative stress.
source: Molecular causes of neurodegeneration are believed to include protein misfolding and degradation, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, DNA damage accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, as well as programmed cell death (Palop et al., 2006; Gan et al., 2018; Kurtishi et al., 2019; Burté et al., 2015; Chi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms have been linked to brain development and neurological disorders.
source: Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding or small RNAs, have been linked to brain development and neurological disorders, such as autism, intellectual disability (ID), and epilepsy, as well as neurodegenerative processes (Meaney and Ferguson-Smith, 2010; Berson et al., 2018; Christopher et al., 2017; Tapias and Wang, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: TRRAP interacts with E2F1 and c-Myc at gene promoters.
source: TRRAP (transformation/transcription domain-associated protein) interacts with E2F1 and c-Myc at gene promoters and is a critical component shared by several HAT complexes, including those from the GNAT and MYST families, which facilitates the recruitment of HAT complexes to target proteins for acetylation (Tapias and Wang, 2017; Knutson and Hahn, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

source: TRRAP (transformation/transcription domain-associated protein) interacts with E2F1 and c-Myc at gene promoters and is a critical component shared by several HAT complexes, including those from the GNAT and MYST families, which facilitates the recruitment of HAT complexes to target proteins for acetylation (Tapias and Wang, 2017; Knutson and Hahn, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: The complete deletion of Trrap in mice and cells is incompatible with the life of proliferating cells and mouse development.
source: The complete deletion of Trrap in mice and cells is incompatible with the life of proliferating cells and mouse development, because of severe defects in the spindle checkpoint and cell cycle control (Herceg et al., 2001; Dhanalakshmi et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Complete deletion of Trrap causes severe defects in the spindle checkpoint and cell cycle control.
source: The complete deletion of Trrap in mice and cells is incompatible with the life of proliferating cells and mouse development, because of severe defects in the spindle checkpoint and cell cycle control (Herceg et al., 2001; Dhanalakshmi et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: A tissue specific deletion of Trrap in embryonic neural stem cells leads to a dysregulation of the cell cycle length which drives the premature differentiation of neuroprogenitors.
source: A tissue specific deletion of Trrap in embryonic neural stem cells leads to a dysregulation of the cell cycle length which drives the premature differentiation of neuroprogenitors (Tapias et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Missense variants of TRRAP have been reported to associate with neuropathological symptoms, including psychosis, ID, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and epilepsy.
source: In humans, missense variants of TRRAP have been recently reported to associate with neuropathological symptoms, including psychosis, ID, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and epilepsy (Cogné et al., 2019; Mavros et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published clinical studies.

claim: The known function of TRRAP in the mitotic checkpoint and cell cycle control does not apply to postmitotic cells.
source: Because the known function of TRRAP in the mitotic checkpoint and cell cycle control does not apply to postmitotic cells, i.e., neurons, how TRRAP and its mediated HAT regulate adult neuronal fitness and affect neurodegeneration remains elusive.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Trrap deletion in the mouse model causes an age-dependent loss of existing neurons leading to neurodegeneration.
source: We find that Trrap deletion in the mouse model (Mus musculus) causes an age-dependent loss of existing neurons leading to neurodegeneration.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding.

claim: Trrap-HAT specifically regulates the Sp1 pathway that controls various neural processes.
source: We show that Trrap-HAT specifically regulates the Sp1 pathway that controls various neural processes, among which microtubule dynamics is particularly affected.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding.

claim: Among the neural processes controlled by the Sp1 pathway, microtubule dynamics is particularly affected by Trrap deletion.
source: We show that Trrap-HAT specifically regulates the Sp1 pathway that controls various neural processes, among which microtubule dynamics is particularly affected.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding.

claim: The Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis is a novel regulator of neuronal arborization and neuroprotection.
source: Our study discloses the Trrap-HAT-Sp1 axis as a novel regulator of neuronal arborization and neuroprotection.
evidence: The manuscript states this as the main conclusion.

claim: Whole proteomic analysis of P10 Trrap-FBΔ cortices identified 122 out of 6919 proteins to be significantly altered after Trrap deletion (cutoff, q < 0.1).
source: Whole proteomic analysis of P10 Trrap-FBΔ cortices identified 122 out of 6919 proteins to be significantly altered after Trrap deletion (cutoff, q < 0.1) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from proteomics analysis and references figures and supplementary file.

claim: 85% of the proteins altered by Trrap deletion were altered in the same way at the RNA level.
source: Notably, a comparison between RNA-seq and proteomics data sets showed that 85% of the proteins altered by Trrap deletion, i.e., 33 upregulated and 71 downregulated genes, were altered in the same way at the RNA level, which resembled 100% directionality (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from integrated analysis and references figures and supplementary file.

claim: Most changes in the proteome were due to changes in the transcriptome.
source: These results indicate that most changes in the proteome were due to changes in the transcriptome.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the high concordance between RNA-seq and proteomics data.

claim: Transcription factors Sp1 and TCFs appeared to be the most relevant upstream factors mediating transcriptional changes after Trrap deletion.
source: We found that most of these transcriptional changes after Trrap deletion were mediated mainly by limited transcription factors, among which transcription factors Sp1 and TCFs appeared to be the most relevant upstream factors (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from TFBS enrichment analysis and references figure and supplementary file.

claim: Transcription factors TCF1, TCF3, and NFAT are known effectors of the Wnt signaling pathways.
source: Transcription factors TCF1, TCF3, and NFAT are known effectors of the Wnt signaling pathways (Cadigan and Waterman, 2012) and were indeed downstream of the Sp1-mediated transcription regulation upon Trrap deletion (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: TCF1, TCF3, and NFAT were downstream of the Sp1-mediated transcription regulation upon Trrap deletion.
source: Transcription factors TCF1, TCF3, and NFAT are known effectors of the Wnt signaling pathways (Cadigan and Waterman, 2012) and were indeed downstream of the Sp1-mediated transcription regulation upon Trrap deletion (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from analysis of the data.

claim: Sp1 is likely the main regulator for all transcriptional changes in Trrap-deleted brains.
source: Hence, our data suggest that Sp1 is likely the main regulator for all these changes in Trrap-deleted brains.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the TFBS enrichment analysis.

claim: Sp1 is a key transcription factor capable of regulating many cellular processes, including proliferation, cell differentiation, apoptosis, immune responses, DNA damage responses, and chromatin remodeling.
source: Sp1 is a key transcription factor capable of regulating many cellular processes, including proliferation, cell differentiation, apoptosis, immune responses, DNA damage responses, and chromatin remodeling (Li and Davie, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: 1261 common DEGs were found among Trrap-deleted cortices, striata, and aNSCs.
source: We first validated the transcriptome of aNSCs in comparison with that of Trrap-FBΔ cortex and striatum and found 1261 common DEGs among these three samples.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The directionality is very conserved in 93.1% between the cortex and aNSCs.
source: The directionality is very conserved in 93.1% between the cortex and aNSCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c,d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references figure and supplementary file.

claim: Trrap-HAT regulates a very conserved transcriptomic network in different brain regions as well as in NSCs.
source: Thus, Trrap-HAT regulates a very conserved transcriptomic network in different brain regions as well as in NSCs.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the high overlap and directionality conservation of DEGs.

claim: A high degree of the DEGs from Trrap-deleted brains as well as aNSCs were putative Sp1 targets.
source: We found that a high degree of the DEGs from Trrap-deleted brains as well as aNSCs were putative Sp1 targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2f, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from comparison with the Harmonizome database and references figure and supplementary file.

claim: Stathmin family proteins STMN3 and STMN4 are mostly or exclusively expressed in the nervous system.
source: Stathmin family proteins STMN3 and STMN4 are mostly or exclusively expressed in the nervous system where they control microtubule dynamics, an essential process for neuronal differentiation, morphogenesis, and functionality (Chauvin and Sobel, 2015; Dubey et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: STMN3 and STMN4 control microtubule dynamics, an essential process for neuronal differentiation, morphogenesis, and functionality.

evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: The repression of STMN3 suppresses the Purkinje cell neurite growth and arborization.
source: The repression of STMN3 suppresses the Purkinje cell neurite growth and arborization; when overexpressed, it promotes dendritic elongation and branching (Poulain et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: Overexpression of STMN3 promotes dendritic elongation and branching.
source: The repression of STMN3 suppresses the Purkinje cell neurite growth and arborization; when overexpressed, it promotes dendritic elongation and branching (Poulain et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: STMN1 knockout mice showed an age-dependent axonopathy, characterized by a progressive degeneration of axons and demyelination.

evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: An overexpression of STMN2 has been shown to enhance neurite outgrowth by favoring microtubules disassembly.
source: Also, an overexpression of STMN2 has been shown to enhance neurite outgrowth by favoring microtubules disassembly (Morii et al., 2006).

claim: Downregulation of STMN3 and STMN4 is plausibly responsible for axonal swellings and the dendrite retraction of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that downregulation of STMN3 and STMN4 is responsible for axonal swellings and the dendrite retraction of Trrap-deleted Purkinje cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the literature and their findings.

claim: STMN3 and STMN4 express preferentially high during adult life than STMN1 and STMN2 (SCG10).
source: This finding is particularly interesting because that STMN3 and STMN4 express preferentially high during adult life than STMN1 and STMN2 (SCG10), suggesting their important functions in neuronal homeostasis (Chauvin and Sobel, 2015; Voelzmann et al., 2016; Ozon et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: The Trrap-Sp1-mediated transcriptional control of microtubule dynamics plays an instrumental role in neuronal morphogenesis and preventing neurite retraction.
source: Nonetheless, our data demonstrate an instrumental role of the Trrap-Sp1-mediated transcriptional control of microtubule dynamics, likely via STMNs, in neuronal morphogenesis and preventing neurite retraction.
evidence: The manuscript provides this conclusion based on their findings.

claim: The general transcriptional regulator Sp1 is specifically under the control of Trrap-HAT.
